To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the omission of breakfast results in increased hunger and reduced satiety during rest and exercise; (ii) breakfast omission does not affect the energy cost of moderate intensity exercise; and (iii) the omission of a meal results in a blunted response of acylated ghelin and GLP-1(7-36) during exercise.

(i) the effect of breakfast omission on hunger, fullness, energy intake, metabolism, and appetite-related peptides is dependent on the time of day; (ii) the effect of skipping breakfast on hunger, full, and energy intake is greater in the morning than in the evening; (iii) the effect of omitting breakfast on hunger and energy intake is dependent on the timing of the subsequent lunch meal, being greater when the lunch meal is consumed 2 h later; and (iv)

1) the effect of breakfast omission on appetite and metabolism depends on the type and intensity of subsequent exercise; 2) the effects of breakfast omission on hunger and energy intake are similar during exercise of low and high intensity; and 3) the effects of exercise on hunger, energy intake and energy balance differ between breakfast omission and breakfast consumption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the omission of breakfast on the subjective appetite, metabolic rate, acylated-ghrelin and glucagon-like peptide 17-36 (GLP-17- 36).
the effects of breakfast omission on the metabolic, endocrine and subjective appetite responses to exercise and rest in overweight and obese men.
the effects of exercise and diet on appetite and metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
breakfast omission has a negative effect on appetite, energy intake and metabolic responses, which may be exacerbated during exercise.

the effect of breakfast omission on appetite, metabolism, and the hormones ghrelin and glucagon-like peptide-1 (7-36) is not consistent and is dependent upon the type of breakfast, the time of day, and the duration and intensity of the exercise.
the effect of skipping breakfast on appetite and metabolism is not clear, and the effect of skipping lunch is not clear either.

a high-fat diet, which has been shown to increase the risk for cardiovascular disease, can be made healthier by increasing the amount of unsaturated fat.
a breakfast meal is not essential for appetite and metabolism during rest and light exercise.

breakfast omission has no negative effects on appetite or metabolism, but it is associated with a significant increase in the concentration of acylated ghelin, and a decrease in the concentration of active glucagon-like peptide-1 (7-36) during exercise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
eating breakfast is not necessary to lose weight.
eating breakfast can have a positive impact on weight management.
breakfast is an important meal that can have a significant effect on appetite and energy intake.
